title: Research evidence and critical appraisal
blurb: Match research questions to study designs, rank evidence, appraise a study critically, and explain risk to women in a way they can use.
question: A midwife wants to know whether a new perineal massage technique reduces perineal trauma compared with usual care. Which type of single study would give the most reliable answer?

teach.body: SPM 5.16 asks midwives to understand local, national and international research and use it to keep up to date, inform decisions and develop practice. SPM 1.4 asks them to identify, critically analyse and interpret research evidence and data. Code 6.1 says information and advice must be evidence-based. In plain English: you need to know what kind of study answers which question, how much to trust it, and how to explain the results to a woman.

teach.caption: Oxford CEBM levels for questions about treatment effects.

head: Question
Design
rows: Does treatment A work better than B?
What does the whole body of trials show?
Does an exposure lead to an outcome over time?
What was different about cases with a rare outcome?
What is it like for women?

teach.body: Appraisal tools such as CASP checklists ask three broad things. Is the study valid: was it randomised, were groups similar, was follow-up complete, could bias or chance explain the result? What are the results: how big is the effect and how precise (a narrow confidence interval is more precise)? Will it help here: are the women, setting and care similar to yours? A small, uncontrolled or sponsor-run study deserves extra caution.

teach.h: Two ways to describe the same result
teach.caption: NICE NG197: use absolute risk and natural frequencies with the same denominator, and a time period.

teach.body: Hannah, a community midwife, reads an overseas study claiming a supplement halves preterm birth. It followed 60 women, had no control group and was funded by the manufacturer. Appraising it, she notes high risk of bias, a small sample and a different health system. She does not change her advice; she checks NICE and looks for a systematic review, and tells a woman who asks that the evidence is weak and the benefit unproven.

teach.text: Do not confuse the level of evidence with the type of question. An RCT is strongest for 'does it work?', but a qualitative study is the right design for 'what is it like?'. And a dramatic relative risk can hide a tiny absolute difference.

items: For treatment questions: systematic review of RCTs at the top, expert opinion at the bottom.
RCT: does it work; cohort: exposure over time; case-control: rare outcomes; qualitative: experiences.
Appraise: is it valid, what are the results and how precise, will it help here?
Explain risk as absolute numbers and natural frequencies with the same denominator (NICE NG197).
NICE guidance is not mandatory but must be taken fully into account; one weak study does not override it.

summary: You can now choose the right study design for a question, rank evidence and appraise a study for validity, results and applicability. You can also present research findings to women as clear absolute risks.

A.q: For a question about whether a treatment works, which type of evidence is at the top of the hierarchy?
A.why: Oxford CEBM levels: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials is the strongest evidence for treatment effects.

whyNot.0: Cohort studies are observational and rank below RCTs.
whyNot.2: A single RCT ranks below a systematic review of several RCTs.
whyNot.3: Expert opinion is the lowest level.

A.q: A midwife wants to compare two methods of perineal care to see which reduces trauma. Which study design is most appropriate?
A.why: Randomly allocating women to two methods is the best single design to compare treatment effects while minimising bias.

whyNot.0: Qualitative studies explore experiences, not effects.
whyNot.1: Case-control studies look back from an outcome and are weaker for treatment effects.
whyNot.3: Audit measures practice against a standard; it does not compare interventions.

A.q: A midwife wants to understand how women experience being induced. Which study design best answers this?
A.why: Qualitative methods such as interviews explore experiences, meanings and views.

whyNot.1: RCTs measure effects of interventions, not experiences.
whyNot.2: Cohort studies follow outcomes over time, not experiences.

B.q: Researchers want to know whether women who had a stillbirth were more likely to have slept on their back in late pregnancy. Stillbirth is rare. Which design is most efficient?
options: A cross-sectional survey of all women
B.why: Case-control studies start with the outcome (cases and controls) and look back at exposures, which is efficient for rare outcomes.

whyNot.0: It would be unethical to randomise women to sleep positions thought to be harmful.
whyNot.1: Qualitative studies do not measure association.
whyNot.2: A survey of all women would need huge numbers to capture a rare outcome.

B.q: A trial from a country with a very different model of maternity care reports a benefit. What is the key appraisal question before applying it locally?
options: Will the results help women here?
Was it a large international journal?
B.why: Appraisal asks whether the results are valid, what they are, and whether they apply to your women and setting.

whyNot.0: Recency does not tell you whether the results apply.
whyNot.2: Journal prestige is not an appraisal criterion.
whyNot.3: Authors' recommendations do not establish applicability.

B.q: A midwife is explaining the result of a study to a woman. Which way of presenting it best follows NICE NG197?
options: 'It cuts the risk for your baby by half.'
'The risk is significantly lower with it.'
'Experts think it is beneficial for you.'
B.why: NG197: present risk as absolute risk using natural frequencies with a consistent denominator.

whyNot.0: Relative risk on its own can exaggerate the effect.
whyNot.1: 'Significantly' is vague and may be misread.
whyNot.3: Opinion does not tell her the size of the effect.

C.q: A study shows an intervention reduces a complication from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000 births. A woman asks how much difference it makes. What is the most accurate answer?
options: It prevents half of all complications
C.why: The absolute risk reduction is 1 in 1,000; the relative reduction is 50%. NG197 favours absolute figures.

whyNot.0: This is the relative reduction, which can mislead on its own.
whyNot.1: This confuses the 50% relative reduction with an absolute number.
whyNot.2: There is a real, if small, difference.

C.q: A manufacturer-funded study of 40 women with no control group reports a herbal product shortens labour. How should the midwife regard this evidence?
options: As strong, because the effect was large
As strong, as it was published
C.why: Small size, no control group and sponsor funding mean high risk of bias and chance findings. Look for stronger evidence before advising use.

whyNot.0: A large effect in a small biased study is not reliable.
whyNot.3: Weak evidence still informs questions for better research; it is not irrelevant.

C.q: A single new RCT conflicts with current NICE guidance. A colleague says the unit should change practice tomorrow. What is the best response?
options: Follow NICE and evaluate the new evidence
Change practice as the RCT is the newest
Disregard the RCT as NICE takes priority
C.why: One trial rarely outweighs the body of evidence behind a guideline. Continue with guidance while the new evidence is appraised and considered through governance.

whyNot.1: Newest is not the same as strongest; one trial may be an outlier.
whyNot.2: New evidence should be appraised, not dismissed.
whyNot.3: Individual decisions create inconsistent and unsafe care.

reteach.title: Right question, right design
reteach.question: How do you know which study to trust for which question?

blocks.body: Start with the question. Does it work? Look for RCTs and systematic reviews. What causes a rare outcome? Case-control. What happens to people exposed over time? Cohort. What is it like? Qualitative. Then judge quality: bias, size, precision and whether it fits your women and setting.

blocks.text: 'Halves the risk' and '1 fewer in 1,000' can describe the same result.

explain.body: A cohort study follows a group over time, comparing those with and without an exposure (such as smoking in pregnancy) to see who develops an outcome.

test.q: Researchers follow 5,000 pregnant women, comparing smokers and non-smokers, and record birth weights. Which design is this?
test.why: Following exposed and unexposed groups forward to compare outcomes is a cohort study.

whyNot.0: Case-control starts from the outcome and looks back.
whyNot.2: Women were not randomly allocated to smoke.
whyNot.3: Birth weight is a numerical outcome, not an experience.

explain.body: Random allocation makes groups similar in known and unknown factors, so differences in outcome are more likely due to the intervention rather than bias.

test.q: What is the main purpose of randomisation in a trial?
options: To increase the number of participants
To blind participants to the results
To shorten the length of the study
test.why: Randomisation balances known and unknown factors between groups, reducing selection bias.

whyNot.0: Randomisation does not change sample size.
whyNot.3: Randomisation does not shorten a study.

explain.body: A confidence interval shows the range within which the true value is likely to lie. A narrow interval means a more precise estimate, usually from a larger study. MBRRACE-UK's 12.80 per 100,000 came with an interval of 11.27 to 14.48.

test.q: Two studies estimate the same effect. Study A has a much narrower confidence interval than study B. What does this suggest?
options: Study B is more likely to be correct
test.why: A narrower confidence interval means a more precise estimate, usually reflecting a larger sample.

whyNot.1: Narrower intervals usually come from larger, not smaller, samples.
whyNot.2: A wide interval means less certainty, not more accuracy.
whyNot.3: Interval width reflects precision, not design quality as such.

explain.body: NICE guidance is not mandatory; professionals take it fully into account alongside the needs, preferences and values of the individual woman.

test.q: Which statement best describes evidence-based midwifery practice?
options: Doing what the senior midwife prefers
Combining evidence, expertise and her values
test.why: Evidence-based practice combines the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the woman's own values and preferences.

whyNot.0: The latest single study may not be the best evidence.
whyNot.2: Guidance is applied alongside each woman's needs and preferences.
